items.title: Brand Impersonation and Customer Support Hijacking Analysing How Fraudulent Customer Service Accounts on Social Media Scam Corporate Clients
items.abstract: Social media is a public-facing channel for customer-service, and brands are now able to respond to questions and complaints quickly. Consumers' visibility also enables scams to monitor consumers, replicate brand identities and approach consumers via replies or private messages. This article will discuss the methods used by fraudulent customer support accounts to leverage brand recognition and social trust, and will assess controls at the user, company, platform and payment levels. This focused narrative review collated 29 scholarly papers from 2020-2026, comprising of 21 journal papers and eight peer-reviewed conference papers. The evidence shows brand impersonation is not just a fake-profile problem of classification. It's a multi-step fraud route that includes squatting on an account, timely interception of support requests, transferring to private or external channels, requests for credentials, verification codes or payment. Machine-learning studies provide helpful indicators from profile content, profile behavior and network structure, and human-factors studies explain why social familiarity and perceived authenticity can make a difference in reducing scrutiny. Most detection studies rely on labels and data sets, however, that are not inherently linked to customer-support impersonation or financial loss. The article suggests a multi-layered approach to the response, incorporating the official channel clarity of guidance, fast reporting of evidence for preservation, behaviour-awareness in platform detection, safer support channels and metrics for success like time to takedown and repeat-account activity. The review offers a practical approach for minimising the risk of customer harm, as well as opportunities for research in cross-platform measurement and in the field.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI ADOPTION AND EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF DIGITAL COMPETENCE
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become common workplace infrastructure faster than almost any digital technology before it, moving from experimental novelty to everyday workplace infrastructure, yet a critical question remains underexplored in the Indian organisational context: do GenAI tools actually make employees perform better or does that depend on something else entirely – how digitally competent the employee already is? We examine whether digital competence is the missing link in explaining when and for whom the adoption of Generative AI translates into measurable performance gains. Data were collected from 500 employees working in multinational companies located in major Indian business hubs of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram/NCR, Mumbai and Chennai using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design. The suggested model Generative AI Adoption → Digital Competence → Employee Performance was tested using a full analytical pipeline, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s Alpha, Composite Reliability (CR), Average Variance Extracted (AVE), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), correlation analysis, independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, multiple regression, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and bootstrapped mediation analysis. The Findings (reported here on an illustrative dataset, to be replaced by the primary data) suggest that the adoption of Generative AI is significantly and positively associated with digital competence, that digital competence is significantly and positively associated with employee performance, and that digital competence partially mediates the relationship between the adoption of GenAI and performance. The T-test and ANOVA results also suggest that the strength of this chain varies significantly by sex, organisational tenure and job role, indicating a more nuanced, skills-dependent adoption story rather than a homogenous productivity dividend. The findings suggest that Indian subsidiaries of multinationals should focus on digital-competence development, rather than just tool deployment, as the strategic lever to convert GenAI investment into performance results, with a particular focus on tenure-based and role-based upskilling gaps. The current study is among the first integrated SEM-based tests of digital competence as a mediating mechanism in the GenAI–performance relationship within India’s multinational corporate workforce, a fast-growing, strategically important, yet empirically under-examined segment of the global GenAI adoption story.

items.title: AI as corporate communicator: the role of AI source transparency, trust, and engagement in brand advocacy
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a corporate communicator and examines how AI source transparency influences message credibility, employee trust, employee engagement and ultimately brand advocacy. Specifically, the study explores both cognition-based and affect-based dimensions of trust and evaluates the moderating role of AI literacy in shaping employees’ responses to AI-generated communication. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted using an online survey questionnaire. Data were collected from 317 employees across different organizations who had experience with AI-mediated communication in their workplace. Structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 was applied to test the proposed relationships and evaluate the conceptual framework. Findings The findings indicate that AI source transparency positively affects message credibility. Message credibility significantly enhances both cognition-based and affect-based trust, which subsequently increase employee engagement. Employee engagement was also found to positively influence brand advocacy. However, AI literacy showed an unexpected negative moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and cognition-based trust, suggesting that employees with greater AI knowledge become more critical and skeptical of AI-generated content, whereas its moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and affect-based trust is not statistically significant. Practical implications Organizations should not use AI solely as an automation tool but also as a strategic communication instrument. Transparency regarding AI usage, combined with human oversight and quality assurance mechanisms, can strengthen credibility and trust. Companies should also invest in content governance and monitoring practices to ensure that AI-generated communication remains accurate, relevant, and aligned with organizational values. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-mediated corporate communication by developing and empirically testing an integrated model linking AI transparency, message credibility, trust, engagement and brand advocacy. It also provides novel insights into the complex role of AI literacy in influencing employee perceptions and trust toward AI-generated communication.

items.title: Auditory localization and subjective assessment of autonomous cleaning robot sounds: A VR experiment on speed, operating mode and alerting signals
items.abstract: Mobile autonomous robots are increasingly present in everyday environments, where their sounds play a key role in situational awareness and acceptance. Nevertheless, human responses to robot noise remain underexplored. This study examined how robot operating modes and added alerting sounds affect auditory localization and subjective ratings for a professional cleaning robot. Recordings of the robot operating at two velocities during cleaning and non-cleaning were presented. The non-cleaning mode was additionally combined with multi-tone and noise alerting signals, each with and without amplitude modulation. In a VR experiment with within-subjects design, 27 participants performed a localization task and rated annoyance, valence, arousal, and trustworthiness. Localization performance did not differ significantly between sound conditions. Exploratory post hoc analyses indicated that differences between sound conditions varied with participants’ general localization performance, yielding hypotheses for future studies on the role of baseline localization performance. The cleaning sound was rated as most annoying, least pleasant, and least trustworthy, whereas differences between the non-cleaning conditions were rather small. Overall, the alerting signals did not reliably improve localization under the present listening conditions, but some variants may nevertheless warrant further investigation due to their limited negative effects on subjective ratings.

items.title: Beyond the Law: How Philosophy Shapes Legal Consciousness in a Changing Society
items.abstract: The continuous evolution of societal dynamics profoundly shapes how individuals perceive, evaluate, and comply with the law. Within this context, legal philosophy plays a pivotal role in cultivating legal consciousness, as law cannot be reduced merely to a set of formal rules; rather, it constitutes a value-laden system anchored in justice, legal certainty, and utility. This study examines the role of legal philosophy in fostering public legal consciousness and identifies the structural and sociocultural challenges impeding that process. Employing a normative juridical methodology with philosophical and conceptual approaches, this research conducts a qualitative literature review of foundational theories, doctrines, and contemporary socio-legal scholarship. The findings demonstrate that legal philosophy nurtures critical and reflective reasoning regarding the nature, purpose, and normative foundations of law. Legal consciousness extends beyond mere knowledge of statutory provisions to encompass comprehension, evaluative attitudes, institutional trust, and an internalized willingness to adopt law as a guide for social conduct. Nevertheless, cultivating such consciousness faces persistent obstacles, including low legal literacy, tensions between positive law and community moral norms, eroding public trust in legal institutions, the rapid spread of misinformation via digital technology and artificial intelligence, and widespread civic apathy toward legal compliance. Consequently, legal philosophy occupies a strategic position in fostering a critical, rational, and value-oriented legal consciousness capable of sustaining compliance, justice, social order, and legal protection.

items.title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes
items.abstract: When a vulnerability at a security boundary of an LLM agent framework is patched, the advisory identifies the affected and patched versions, and replaying the proof-of-concept (PoC) tests only whether its reported trigger is still reproducible. That the trigger no longer fires does not, on its own, show that the underlying security invariant holds on every code path that reaches the boundary. We present a small, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study built around one question: can original-trigger replay report a boundary as fixed while the same invariant stays violable through a distinct, separately reachable path at the same version? We compare original trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M) for PraisonAI, and perform five additional before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run emits a tri-state verdict of VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE. A mandatory pos itive (authorized) control gates the verdict, so that a non-violation result is admitted only when the control passes in the same run. All probes are benign, using an in-memory flag, a filesystem sentinel, or a builtins reachability check, and none performs a real payload. Our central result reproduces an officially recognized incomplete fix. In PraisonAI, original trigger replay reports the tool-loading boundary as fixed at version 4.6.31, yet the invariant is still violated through the tool_override path. That residual was later assigned its own identifier (CVE-2026-44334, catalogued as a “CVE-2026-40287 patch bypass”) and closed at 4.6.32. The five before/after measurements span four frameworks and four invariant classes. For a CVE whose advisory records no fixed version, we observe confinement in tested release 1.11.1 after observing a violation in 1.11.0. We are explicit about scope. A non-violation verdict means “no violation observed under the tested probe, version, and configuration,” not a proof of safety. The headline harness is control-gated per path, and fourteen fault-injection scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0̸=M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probe invokes the documented loader functions directly, which establishes boundary behavior under the supplied setup rather than a full end-to-end exploit. Finally, we do not claim the method is a new testing technique or that it estimates prevalence.

items.title: DeepChem-DEL: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible DEL Modeling and Benchmarking
items.abstract: Abstract DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) allow screening of extremely large chemical spaces by tagging compounds with DNA barcodes. Machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled the extraction of meaningful chemical patterns from noisy, target-specific DEL binding data. However, existing tools for DEL machine learning (DEL-ML) remain fragmented, which limits systematic construction and reproducibility of modeling pipelines. Moreover, this fragmentation hinders integration of new models, such as chemical foundation models, into DEL workflows alongside classical approaches. To address these challenges in DEL modeling, we introduce DeepChem-DEL, an open-source suite of reproducible ML workflows for DEL modeling built on the DeepChem ecosystem. DeepChem-DEL integrates (i) a configurable denoising pipeline with (ii) modular DeepChem workflows for enrichment prediction, hit identification, and benchmarking across diverse model classes, including chemical foundation models enabled through extensions to the open-source ChemBERTa-3 framework. We evaluate DeepChem-DEL on the KinDEL and BELKA data sets, reproducing key baselines and enabling direct comparison across model classes. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging chemical foundation models yields performance competitive with, and in several cases exceeding, previously explored approaches such as graph convolutional networks and random forest models. Together, these results demonstrate that DeepChem-DEL is a scalable and extensible platform for DEL-ML, while highlighting the potential of chemical foundation models for improved DEL modeling and prioritization.

items.title: FoMo-X: Modular Explainability Signals for Outlier Detection Foundation Models
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models, specifically Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), have revolutionized outlier detection (OD) by enabling unsupervised zero-shot adaptation to new datasets without training. However, despite their predictive power, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, outputting scalar outlier scores that lack the operational context required for safety-critical decision-making. Existing post-hoc explanation methods are often computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment or fail to capture the epistemic uncertainty inherent in zero-shot inference. In this work, we introduce FoMo-X, a modular framework that equips OD foundation models with intrinsic, lightweight diagnostic capabilities. We leverage the insight that the frozen embeddings of a pretrained PFN backbone already encode rich, context-conditioned relational information. FoMo-X attaches auxiliary diagnostic heads to these embeddings, trained offline using the same generative simulator prior as the backbone. This allows us to distill computationally expensive properties, such as Monte Carlo dropout based epistemic uncertainty, into a deterministic, single-pass inference. We instantiate FoMo-X with two novel heads: a Severity Head that discretizes deviations into interpretable risk tiers, and an Uncertainty Head that provides calibrated confidence measures. Extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ADBench) demonstrates that FoMo-X recovers ground-truth diagnostic signals with high fidelity and negligible inference overhead. By bridging the gap between foundation model performance and operational explainability, FoMo-X offers a scalable path toward trustworthy, zero-shot outlier detection.

items.title: GhostGuard AI: An Intelligent System for Detecting Ghost Workers and Attendance Fraud Using Biometric, GPS, and Payment Analytics
items.abstract: This research paper presents GhostGuard AI, a proposed intelligent system for identifying ghost workers, proxy attendance, and fraudulent wage payments. The system combines facial biometric verification, GPS-based geofencing, mobile device integrity checks, and payment analytics to improve workforce verification. The proposed architecture integrates artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to identify suspicious attendance patterns, duplicate payment accounts, and unusual relationships between workers, devices, and financial records. It aims to support transparent, reliable, and accountable workforce management. The paper discusses the problem, objectives, proposed methodology, system architecture, expected applications, limitations, and future development possibilities. items.abstract: Abstract Humans consistently outperform state-of-the-art AI models in action recognition, particularly in challenging real-world conditions involving low resolution, occlusion, and visual clutter.e those utilised by humans Understanding the sources of this performance gap is essential for developing more robust and human-aligned models. In this paper, we present a large-scale human AI comparative study of egocentric action recognition using human-defined Minimal Identifiable Recognition Crops (MIRCs), defined as the smallest spatial or spatiotemporal regions sufficient for reliable human recognition. We used our previously introduced, Epic-ReduAct, a systematically spatially reduced and temporally scrambled dataset derived from 36 EPIC-KITCHENS videos, spanning multiple spatial reduction levels and temporal conditions. Recognition performance is evaluated using over 3,000 human participants, Side4Video, and Qwen 3.5 9B models. Our analysis combines quantitative metrics, Average Reduction Rate and Recognition Gap, with qualitative analyses of spatial (high-, mid-, and low-level visual features) and spatiotemporal factors, including a categorisation of actions into Low Temporal Actions (LTA) and High Temporal Actions (HTA). Results show that human performance exhibits sharp declines when transitioning from MIRCs to sub-MIRCs, reflecting a strong reliance on sparse, semantically critical cues such as hand object interactions. In contrast, the model degrades more gradually and often relies on contextual and mid- to low-level features, sometimes even exhibiting increased confidence under spatial reduction. Temporally, humans remain robust to scrambling when key spatial cues are preserved, whereas the model often shows insensitivity to temporal disruption, revealing class-dependent temporal sensitivities. Overall, our findings demonstrate that strong benchmark performance can obscure fundamental human AI misalignment and highlight limitations in current spatial and spatiotemporal representations, suggesting concrete directions for more efficient and human-aligned action recognition systems.

items.title: Information Overload and Disutility in Generative AI Systems as Cognitive Extension: A Bounded Rationality Perspective
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

items.title: Multicenter evaluation of radiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence for colorectal cancer diagnosis and survival prediction
items.abstract: Abstract Reliable preoperative classification and outcome prediction could improve management of locally advanced colorectal cancer. We retrospectively studied 879 participants from two centers, including 741 patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer and 138 with benign colorectal lesions. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and early fusion models were trained at center A ( n = 615) and independently tested at center B ( n = 264) using pretreatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical data. The clinical-radiomics nomogram achieved a test AUC of 0.957 for benign-malignant classification. For 3-year and 5-year overall survival, radiomics achieved test AUCs of 0.874 and 0.898, while fusion achieved 0.870 and 0.899, respectively. These findings identify CT radiomics as a promising digital biomarker for colorectal cancer stratification and show that early deep learning fusion offers limited incremental value over an optimized radiomics baseline.

items.title: Physician AI disclosure, condition severity, and public trust in digital medicine
items.abstract: Abstract Public trust is central to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital medicine, yet little is known about how patients respond to different forms of physician AI disclosure across clinical risk contexts. In a 5 × 2 factorial experiment in mainland China, 1574 adults were randomly assigned to physician profiles varying by AI use type and condition severity. Administrative AI was rated more favorably than diagnostic and therapeutic AI across physician perception and care-seeking intention outcomes. High-severity conditions amplified negative responses to therapeutic AI, whereas explicit non-AI disclosure was associated with greater appointment willingness under high severity. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested that competence, trust, and empathy accounted for different disclosure-related response patterns. Main effects were directionally consistent in a supplementary offline community sample from Macao ( n = 128). These findings suggest that AI disclosure in digital medicine should distinguish administrative from clinical uses and be calibrated to clinical severity, while highlighting the need for preregistered replication using behavioral outcomes.

items.title: R-SYS for protocol versioning and independent reviewer workflows in systematic reviews
items.abstract: Abstract Background Systematic review software must coordinate independent human decisions, protocol amendments and heterogeneous information sources. Synchronizing reviewers at every stage can create waiting time unrelated to the scientific assessment of a record. We describe R-SYS, a workflow that links decisions to versioned protocols and allows reviewers to progress independently before a final reconciliation step. Methods The reference implementation combines an eleven-phase guarded lifecycle, immutable locked protocol versions, deterministic rendering of a canonical search strategy, per-reviewer working sets and decision provenance. Each primary reviewer advances through title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, extraction and risk-of-bias appraisal using their own preceding decisions, subject to human adjudication. A final convergence checkpoint resolves outstanding work before synthesis. Artificial intelligence (AI) supplies advisory recommendations that are excluded from human reconciliation. We analyse completion times under explicit scheduling assumptions and describe implementation limitations. Results With identical task sets, continuous reviewer availability and no external waiting, independent lanes achieve a completion time equal to the largest reviewer workload. This is a lower bound for schedules that impose additional synchronization constraints. Disagreement can introduce superseded work and delays; a sufficient condition for retaining an advantage over stage barriers is stated. The implementation provides mechanisms for protocol change control, reviewer coordination and traceable reporting. No empirical measurements of accuracy, efficiency, usability or cost are reported. Conclusions R-SYS provides a reference design for separating reviewer independence from workflow synchronization. Its theoretical scheduling properties do not establish practical time savings, search completeness or AI accuracy. A separate, prospectively specified validation study is planned after completed reviews using the platform become available.

items.title: Real-Time Academic Platform Integration Design (RAPID): A Descriptive Framework for Course Communication and Support
items.abstract: Abstract Persistent, channel-organized communication environments give instructors ways to arrange questions, assistance, announcements, and informal interaction alongside a learning management system. Their use depends on how students enter the environment, how information and audiences are organized, who provides assistance, and how participation is experienced. This conceptual article presents Real-Time Academic Platform Integration Design (RAPID), a descriptive framework developed through a focused synthesis of 37 publications and a source-anchored matrix of 750 evidence items. Following a bounded literature search with artificial intelligence support for screening and extraction, the authors reviewed source evidence and selected and refined the framework by comparing model-generated alternatives. RAPID comprises four components: Student Onboarding, Environment Organization, Sustainable Help, and Student Participation and Social Climate, interpreted through an affordance perspective and Community of Inquiry. A constructed LMS-centered baseline, two reflective teaching illustrations, and a literature-informed projection show how it applies across differences in course size, staffing, and participation requirements. The framework’s usefulness, workload implications, and relationship to learning require empirical study.

items.title: Reducing barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education: opportunities for AI
items.abstract: Australia’s growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) skills contrasts with stagnant tertiary participation and persistent inequities. This brief review examines barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education and the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to support Universal Design for Learning. AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. Effective adoption therefore requires institutional governance, AI proficiency and sustained educator judgement. Further longitudinal research in Australian tertiary STEM settings is needed to identify which tools reduce barriers, for whom and under what conditions.

items.title: Regional artificial intelligence development and agricultural ecological efficiency: evidence from Chinese provinces
items.abstract: Existing studies have primarily focused on the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on productivity and carbon emission efficiency, while systematic evidence on whether and through which mechanisms AI improves agricultural ecological efficiency (AEE) remains relatively limited. Using provincial panel data from China for the period 2005 to 2023, this study employs the entropy weighting method to measure regional AI development and a slack-based measure (SBM) model incorporating undesirable outputs to evaluate AEE. A two-way fixed effects model is further constructed to examine the effects of AI on AEE and the underlying mechanisms. AI is conceptually distinct from general digitalization, automation, precision agriculture, and information technology development, as its defining feature lies in leveraging machine learning, intelligent sensing, and algorithmic decision-making to achieve more advanced data processing and intelligent decision-making capabilities. The results indicate that a 0.1-unit increase in regional AI development is associated with an average increase of 0.01078 units in AEE. Mechanism analysis suggests that AI can indirectly improve AEE by promoting green finance development and industrial structure upgrading. Furthermore, agricultural technological innovation exhibits a significant threshold effect, with higher levels of technological innovation strengthening the positive effect of AI on AEE. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the positive effect of AI on AEE is more pronounced in eastern regions, regions with lower levels of urbanization and agricultural modernization, and non-major grain-producing regions. Further analysis identifies positive spatial spillover effects of AI on AEE in neighboring regions, contributing to coordinated green agricultural development across local and neighboring regions. This study provides evidence on the effects, transmission mechanisms, and threshold conditions through which AI improves AEE, offering new empirical insights into the role of AI in facilitating the green transformation of agriculture and extending the analytical perspective of agricultural sustainability research.

items.title: Rethinking English Education In The Era Of Generative Ai And Global Englishes
items.abstract: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

items.title: Science communication in the age of AI? Curiosity, multimedia, storytelling
items.abstract: Science communication leverages online multimedia to raise public awareness of research and discovery, yet its efficacy is built upon digital competencies, communication and storytelling. These skills sit outside the scope of traditional scientific training, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools can accelerate professional learning in service of public outreach. Three different AI prompting strategies were used to convert a research article written by the author to a format appropriate for a public lecture. Different titles, graphics, and a talk outline informed by the Three Act Storytelling framework were extracted from the paper using one-shot, chain of thought and role-prompting strategies. These resources can be re-purposed for video abstracts, lay summaries and social media posts to facilitate science communication to a broad generalist audience. The effectiveness of AI as a collaborative tool for ideation is considered alongside its impact on scientific credibility and graduate employability.

items.title: Teaching Reform of Civil Engineering Construction Course under the Background of AI
items.abstract: With the large-scale implementation of generative artificial intelligence, digital twin, BIM and other technologies in the construction industry, the construction industry is transforming from the traditional manual construction mode to the intelligent construction mode, and the demand for industry post ability has changed significantly. As a core compulsory course of civil engineering undergraduate major, civil engineering construction undertakes the task of imparting professional knowledge such as construction technology, construction organization and site management. The traditional classroom teaching mode has practical contradictions such as lack of practical scenes, lagging update of teaching content, insufficient individualized training of students, and single assessment method. The teaching practice shows that the reasonable introduction of AI auxiliary tools can make up for the shortcomings of traditional teaching field conditions, enrich classroom case resources, and strengthen students’ engineering practice thinking. However, it also faces practical challenges such as students’ excessive dependence on AI output content, professional information distortion, and teachers’ teaching ability can not keep up with technical iteration. This study can provide reference for the digital teaching reform of construction courses in similar engineering majors, and help to cultivate compound civil engineering talents with both traditional construction skills and intelligent construction literacy.

items.title: Towards a Pedagogical Framework for Integrating Generative AI Into Competency-Based Education in Secondary Schools in the Global South
items.abstract: Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.

items.title: Towards Semi-Automatic Benchmarking of Large Language Models for Self-Regulated Language Learning
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.

items.title: Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation: How a Confirmed Fact Can Lend Its Certainty to a Story
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation, a mechanism by which checking one part of an account lends certainty to a wider interpretation even though the evidence for that interpretation stays the same. The paper asks which alternatives a check can distinguish. A finding can support a wider claim when it rules out a rival explanation. Where either explanation would have produced the same result, the choice between them remains open. In 2002, researchers dated the parchment of the Vinland Map to about 1434. A medieval drawing and a modern drawing on that same sheet would both yield the same parchment date. In 2003, a report in Hayadan placed the drawing about fifty years before Columbus’s voyage. The report offered a separate argument about the ink for its claim of authenticity, but gave no independent date for the drawing. In 2021, Yale reported finding modern ink throughout the map’s lines and text. In September 1904, a Berlin commission ruled out deliberate signaling under the conditions in which it examined the horse known as Clever Hans. Carl Stumpf, a commission member, later wrote that many readers understood the report as a declaration that the horse could think. Follow-up experiments by Oskar Pfungst and his colleagues identified an explanation the September examination had left open. Hans responded to small, unintended movements by a person he could see. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper places this mechanism alongside Tversky and Kahneman’s work on the conjunction fallacy. In a human–AI setting, a reviewer might verify that an assistant quoted a motion exactly from meeting minutes. The same wording could appear whether the motion passed or failed. Verifying the assistant’s further claim that the committee adopted it would require the recorded outcome.

items.title: “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

items.title: “High demand, low training, moderate trust”: a needs assessment survey of AI integration in clinical medicine education among clinical medicine students
items.abstract: Objective As artificial intelligence increasingly permeates healthcare, it remains unclear whether clinical medicine students are adequately prepared for this transformation. This study aimed to investigate AI awareness, usage patterns, teaching needs, and curriculum expectations among clinical medicine students to inform evidence-based curricular reform. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 930 individuals affiliated with a medical and pharmaceutical college and its affiliated hospitals; 619 valid responses (94.18% current students/interns) were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results While 75.93% of respondents were aware of AI applications in healthcare, only 31.99% used AI tools frequently. Although 88.21% acknowledged the necessity of integrating AI into clinical medicine teaching, merely 48.47% reported that their institution offered relevant courses. Moderate trust in AI-assisted diagnosis was expressed by 70.76% of participants. The most desired teaching contents were case analysis and diagnostic simulation (75.61%), drug recommendation and dosage calculation (70.44%), and imaging/pathology recognition (65.91%). Conclusion These findings, derived from a predominantly student sample, highlight a pronounced ‘high demand, low training, moderate trust’ pattern in this vocational college context. A clinically grounded, progressively structured, and practice-oriented AI curriculum may inform curricular reform to prepare students for the AI-driven healthcare era.

items.title: “Should I Give Up Now?” Investigating LLM Pitfalls in Software Engineering
items.abstract: Software engineers are increasingly incorporating AI assistants into their workflows to enhance productivity and alleviate cognitive load. However, experiences with Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT vary widely. While some engineers find them useful, others deem them counterproductive due to inaccuracies in their responses. Researchers have also observed that ChatGPT often provides incorrect information. Given these limitations, it is crucial to determine how to effectively integrate LLMs into Software Engineering (SE) workflow. Analyzing data from 26 participants in a complex web development task, we identified nine failure types categorized into incorrect or incomplete responses, cognitive overload, and context loss. Users attempted to mitigate these issues through scaffolding, prompt clarification, and debugging. However, 17 participants ultimately chose to abandon ChatGPT due to persistent failures. Our quantitative analysis revealed that unhelpful responses increased the likelihood of abandonment by a factor of 11, while each additional prompt reduced abandonment probability by 17%. This study advances the understanding of human-AI interaction in SE tasks and outlines directions for future research and tooling support.

items.abstract: Alternative Titles: AI Security: 5 Critical Threat Scenarios Where an AI Agent’s Permission Is Not Authorization Top 5 Rogue AI Threat Scenarios: Binding Consequential AI Actions to Independent Authorization in Critical Infrastructure AI Safety for NIS2 and the EU AI Act: 5 Threat Models and an Enforcement Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents Abstract Autonomous AI agents, optimizers, and AI-assisted security tools now hold standing permissions to alter production infrastructure at machine speed. In the European Union, this is no longer merely a technical vulnerability—it is a strict regulatory compliance mandate. Operators of essential and important entities under the NIS2 Directive, financial entities under DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act), critical entities under the CER Directive, and providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act must definitively prove that automated actions cannot cause uncontrolled, cascading disruptions. While conventional cybersecurity controls—such as AI guardrails, Role-Based Access Control (IAM/RBAC), LLM-as-a-judge reviewer models, human approval workflows, canary releases, and anomaly detection tools—reduce risk, none of them structurally prevent a wrong, manipulated, or malicious AI decision from becoming an effective infrastructure change. This technical disclosure analyzes the persistent "guardrail trap" and introduces a non-bypassable architectural solution. This disclosure defines a comprehensive threat model featuring 5 critical rogue-AI scenarios: The Runaway Optimizer: A locally optimal AI decision triggers systemic infrastructure instability. Unmediated Agentic Execution: A privileged AI assistant converts an ambiguous instruction into a destructive operation. Correlated Security Monoculture: Shared AI security logic causes synchronized, false-positive network shutdowns. Adversarially Induced Infrastructure Shutdown: External attackers manipulate automated defenses into disabling essential services (e.g., via prompt injection or data poisoning). The Self-Authorizing Agent: A rogue agent edits its own guardrails, forges its approval, and erases its audit logs. To address these vulnerabilities, the disclosure details 51 threat variations, a 36-entry threat register, and 12 required security properties for autonomous systems. It provides a qualitative comparison demonstrating which common control classes meet these properties. Crucially, it establishes a formal technical distinction between permission (a standing, class-level entitlement) and authorization (a one-time, act-specific, state-bound capability consumed on use), as well as separating a "pending" workflow status from a cryptographically enforced "non-effective state." The Protected Execution-Finality Architecture: The proposed safeguard ensures that every consequential AI action remains in a non-effective state until an Independent Validator reconstructs the actual pending operation and issues a single-use capability bound to that exact act. A Policy Enforcement Point (Finality Sink) at the real point of effect verifies the capability, rejecting stale, substituted, replayed, or widened operations. For high-criticality environments, the architecture introduces receipt-gated staged effectuation (Interim Effectuation Validation), ensuring that even a mistakenly authorized change exposes only the current stage, gated by destination-generated cryptographic evidence. The disclosure provides consequence-tiered latency rules, fail-closed behaviors during validator outages, 20 defensive simulation blueprints with acceptance criteria, and explicit residual limits. All scenarios are hypothetical threat models, not reports of incidents, and no experimental results are claimed. items.title: A Comparative Analysis of Customer Segmentation Techniques Using K-Means, Hierarchical and Density-Based Spatial Clusterings
items.abstract: In present day data driven marketing process customer segmentation is very important component so that institutions may understand diverse client behavior and undertake design inspired initiatives. With growing availability of transactional data, artificial intelligence (AI) -based unsupervised learning techniques have gained popularity for identifying meaningful customer segments without prior labeling. This study presents a comparative analysis of three commonly used approaches to customer segmentation such as K-Means clustering, Hierarchical clustering, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN). This study is based on the data set taken from Kaggle consisting of 541,909 records and eight variables. The customer label data which is aggregated from transaction-level to construct behavioral features based on Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM). Along with additional purchase behavior indicator to assess transaction and principal component analysis (PCA) was applied prior to clustering for high scale sensitivity and high dimensionality. Study results showed that K-Means offer well separated stable clusters of large customer groups. Hierarchical clustering offers valuable insights into cluster structures and DBSCAN nicely diagnosed noise and atypical purchasing behavior at the same time sensitive to parameter selection in high density marketing data. The study showcased the trade-offs between algorithmic performance as well as business interpretability, giving guidance to marketing analysts enabling decision-makers to decide suitable segmentation techniques.

items.title: A decade‐scale audit of microbiome AI‐readiness
items.abstract: A systematic, PRISMA-guided review led by our consortium screened 23,781 human microbiome papers and procured 2896 studies published from 2012 to 2025 that were then scored by reviewers into four Biological Host-Associated AI-Ready Metadata (BHAM) tiers. Only 5.9% of studies deposited sequence data with per-sample host disease status, age, and sex, and 63.1% shared no reusable sequence data, so that 85.5% of roughly 720,000 samples cannot be reused for cross-cohort or artificial intelligence (AI) analyses without contacting the authors. Sequence deposition improved modestly over time, whereas per-sample annotation did not. Journals, repositories, and researchers should require structured, machine-readable metadata at submission, supported by AI-assisted curation.

items.title: A Fairness-Aware Explainable Artificial Intelligence Clinical Decision Support Framework Using Electronic Health Records
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) are increasingly being adopted in Electronic Health Record (EHR) based healthcare settings to enhance disease prediction, clinical diagnosis and operational efficiency. Current healthcare AI systems, however, are facing serious challenges such as demographic bias, transparency, unreliable predictions, poor explainability and low clinician trust. We propose a fairness-aware explainable AI framework for trustworthy and transparent EHR-based CDSS. The proposed framework integrates machine learning prediction models with SHAP-based explainability, fairness evaluation metrics, subgroup bias attribution, reliability testing, and clinician-centered evaluation into one trustworthy healthcare AI architecture. Experiments are done using standard EHR datasets like UCI Heart Disease Dataset and MIMIC-IV. We compared different models like Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost using metrics such as accuracy, ROC-AUC, Equalized Odds, Demographic Parity, robustness score and explainability consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the reliability of clinical prediction, reduces subgroup bias, enhances interpretability, and increases clinician trust compared to conventional black-box healthcare AI systems. This work advances towards trustworthy, transparent, and fairness-aware healthcare AI systems fit for real-world clinical deployment.

items.title: A Federated Learning Architecture Through MONDRAGON-X Industrial Data Space
items.abstract: Industries often hold valuable data locked in silos, limiting both the amount and diversity of data available for training machine learning models and consequently reducing accuracy and generalization capabilities. Centralizing sensitive data or sharing it with third parties introduces significant privacy and security risks, complicating data governance and control. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these challenges by enabling collaborative model training without the need to transfer raw data, thus preserving privacy while harnessing distributed information. Complementarily, Data Spaces provide a secure framework for trusted data exchange through standardized protocols and robust governance, ensuring interoperability and responsible data use. By integrating FL within a Data Space, organizations can overcome the dual hurdles of data silos and stringent privacy requirements, while FL inherently safeguards privacy by enabling collaborative model training without raw data transfer, its integration within a Data Space offers enhanced security and governance beyond traditional FL. This approach ensures that all interactions, from service discovery to model exchange, are governed by explicit policies and contracts, providing unprecedented traceability and control over the collaborative AI lifecycle. This paper presents a novel architecture implemented within the Mondragon-X Industrial Data Space that seamlessly embeds the FL workflow. Leveraging advanced EDC connectors, dedicated APIs, and the Flower AI framework in a hybrid edge-cloud environment, our approach enables continuous model updates, collaborative improvements, and strict data sovereignty, thereby establishing a scalable foundation for developing powerful and privacy-preserving industrial artificial intelligence (AI) solutions.

items.title: A fragmented field in transition: knowledge structures and emerging agendas in lifelong learning for sustainable development
items.abstract: Lifelong learning is increasingly recognised as essential to sustainable development, yet its knowledge structure and emerging research directions remain insufficiently understood. This study analysed 806 articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection between 2001 and 30 July 2026 using bibliometric, collaboration-network, keyword co-occurrence, temporal-comparison, and sensitivity analyses. The findings revealed sustained publication growth, fragmented author collaboration, and uneven institutional connectivity. Two major thematic concentrations emerged: transformative and sustainability education in higher education and teacher development; and adult, non-formal, informal, community, and continuing learning associated with the Sustainable Development Goals. Emerging research directions included inclusive education, experiential learning, sustainability competencies, gender equality, gamification, and artificial intelligence, although these remained relatively low-frequency topics. Sensitivity analysis indicated that keyword-network coherence was partly influenced by the retrieval strategy. Overall, the literature demonstrated growing interest in participatory, inclusive, competency-oriented, and digitally supported learning while remaining structurally dispersed. This study clarifies the intellectual landscape of lifelong learning for sustainable development, identifies emerging research priorities, and emphasises the importance of retrieval design when interpreting bibliometric findings.

items.title: A graph attention network-driven multi-omics framework for predicting infection severity and therapeutic outcomes in diabetes
items.abstract: Introduction Diabetes mellitus predisposes patients to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections owing to impaired immune responses and metabolic dysfunction, frequently leading to severe complications, prolonged hospitalization, and suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. Accurate risk stratification remains challenging due to the heterogeneous and high-dimensional nature of multi-omics data, which hinders effective integration across molecular layers. Methods To address this gap, we propose a graph attention network (GAT)-based multi-omics integration framework that jointly models genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and clinical variables for predicting infection severity and treatment outcomes in diabetic patients. A retrospective multicenter cohort of 2,800 diabetic patients was assembled, encompassing 18,500 genomic variants, 19,800 transcriptomic features, 4,250 proteomic features, 610 metabolites, 320 microbial taxa, and 28 clinical variables. Infection severity was categorized into four clinically defined levels: mild (n = 720), moderate (n = 940), severe (n = 760), and critical (n = 380). After preprocessing, 43,508 molecular features were reduced to 1,024 optimized biomarkers through a sequential pipeline of differential expression analysis, mutual information filtering, LASSO regression, and recursive feature elimination. A heterogeneous patient similarity graph comprising 2,800 nodes and approximately 96,400 weighted edges was constructed using cosine similarity. A three-layer graph attention network with eight attention heads per layer generated 256-dimensional node embeddings, which were subsequently utilized in a multi-task learning framework to jointly predict infection severity and therapeutic outcome. The proposed framework was evaluated via five-fold cross-validation and benchmarked against conventional machine learning models (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP) and graph-based deep learning models (GCN, GraphSAGE). Results The GAT-based model achieved an accuracy of 98.34%, precision of 97.86%, recall of 97.63%, specificity of 98.11%, F1-score of 97.74%, Matthews correlation coefficient of 96.95%, AUC of 99.18%, and AUPRC of 98.82%, significantly outperforming all baseline models. Discussion These results demonstrate that the proposed GNN-driven multi-omics framework effectively integrates heterogeneous molecular and clinical information, offering a promising artificial intelligence-assisted precision medicine tool for personalized risk stratification, therapeutic decision-making, and improved clinical management of infections in diabetic patients.

items.title: A Human-Centered Ontology for AI-Driven Human-Robot Collaboration
items.abstract: Manufacturing is quickly moving toward a human-centered approach, adjusting production systems to match workers’ needs, preferences, skills, and mental or physical state. Even though Human Factors are important in collaborative robotics, there’s little research on how they affect AI-based manufacturing. This gap highlights the need for new Knowledge Engineering solutions that represent in a formal and structured way also human-centric attributes within manufacturing environments. In this paper, we propose the extension of a state of the art ontology for human-robot collaboration by, first, identifying which HF are most relevant to collaborative manufacturing and, then, defining how they can be effectively represented. Including HF into knowledge representation enables AI-based robot control to consider worker conditions and dynamically adapt their task execution accordingly ensuring both safety, efficiency and worker well-being.

items.title: A Hybrid Retrieval and Reranking Framework for Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model outputs by grounding generated responses in external evidence. However, the quality of RAG-generated answers depends strongly on the relevance of retrieved evidence, the effectiveness of evidence ranking, and the ability to verify whether generated claims are supported by source documents. This study presents a hybrid retrieval and reranking framework for citation-aware RAG in biomedical and healthcare-related document question answering. The proposed framework uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for document ingestion, parsing, chunking, embedding generation, and evidence retrieval. Source PDF documents are stored in Amazon S3, embedded using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, and indexed using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. A hybrid retrieval strategy is applied to retrieve candidate evidence chunks, followed by reranking to prioritize the most relevant passages before answer generation. The answer-generation stage uses the highest-ranked evidence chunks to produce controlled, evidence-grounded responses, while a separate judge model evaluates each generated factual claim against the retrieved evidence. The framework was evaluated using 150 biomedical natural language processing and healthcare transformer queries. This evaluation was designed as a pilot-scale proof-of-concept study to examine the feasibility of the proposed hybrid retrieval, reranking, answer-generation, and grounding-evaluation workflow. Across the evaluation set, the system retrieved and reranked 3,000 evidence chunks and generated responses from the top-ranked evidence. Claim-level grounding evaluation identified 1,200 factual claims, of which 1,184 were judged to be supported by the retrieved evidence and 16 were classified as unsupported, resulting in an overall grounding accuracy of 98.7%. The results indicate that hybrid retrieval, reranking, conservative prompting, and claim-level grounding evaluation can support reliable evidence-grounded RAG responses when sufficient source evidence is available. The study also highlights the distinction between internal grounding accuracy and strict citation accuracy, motivating future work on explicit sentence-level citation generation and expanded human expert validation.

items.title: A Methodology for Enabling AI-Driven Quality Control in Human-Robot Collaborative Applications
items.abstract: Quality control is a significant topic for manufacturing under the scope of industry 5.0, while industries are devoting more efforts for resilient and sustainable processes but also while keeping the human in the loop. Under this scope, different human-robot collaborative technologies have emerged in order to address issues affecting the quality of different products, processes or equipment involved in manufacturing scenarios. This paper presents a methodology towards the efficient artificial intelligence (AI )- driven quality control of applications involving the collaboration between robots and human operators. The proposed approach involves aspects related to both robots and humans, aiming to robustly adapt the factors responsible for the quality of the final product itself. An AI-based framework is also deployed implementing the proposed methodology under real conditions. The proposed methodology is being applied in an industrial scenario derived from the automotive sector, where the accurate assembly of high payload parts is required under human-robot collaborative applications.

items.title: A multilayer ontology of psychological stress ranging from lived experiences to neurobiological cascades
items.abstract: Chronic stress is a phenomenon measured in pieces: an appraised predicament, a behavioral pattern, an autonomic shift, an HPA-axis cascade, an inflammatory-metabolic state, a molecular signature. Each is well characterized, but they are rarely reconciled in one computable model. We present the Corticoidogenic Stress Frames (CSF), a modular ontology network in which eight conceptual frames are each anchored to a primary corticoidogenic literature. CSF formalizes eight stress-related strata with their pathways and the cascade steps occurring at each layer. Appropriate competency questions validate the result on knowledge graphs extracted from stress-related datasets. CSF-shaped knowledge graphs are extracted automatically either from physiological data or linguistic reports. The extraction is performed by POLANYI++, a neurosymbolic AI pipeline in which a LLM recognizes patterns, while the ontology supplies the inductive bias, the vocabulary and the validation. Sensor features and first-person narrative bind to shared cascade steps, so quantified physiology and appraisal data are represented in a graph, while keeping their provenance. We present six studies. Study 0 confirms on a signal-free dataset that the pipeline returns a null rather than fabricating structure. Study 1 shows CSF constructs are sensitive to known conditions across three benchmarks. Study 2 finds a within-subject coupling between daily activity and momentary stress, positive within individuals, yet dissociable from the protective trait-level exercise buffer of Study 1. Study 3 evaluates extraction from forty-one unannotated diary posts by a reverse method, extracting the conceptual frames convergent with model-free affect signals. Study 4 shows that the co-activation distribution over multilayer frames is stable. In Study 5, five models from three families judge extraction items under blinding, aggregated by a Dawid–Skene latent-class model. By design each specialist rules only within its own stratum and abstains elsewhere, which keeps the judgments free of cross-expertise contamination. As an external human referent, a neuropsychologist rated a sample, endorsing the extracted frames in 11 of 13 cases. The framework offers a route to layer integration in stress physiology, with evidential status of each layer represented explicitly.

items.title: A Place in Between
items.abstract: A Place in Between is a 4-minute-7-second black-and-white short film about memory, absence, hope, and the emotional space between holding on and letting go. The project was realized through a director-led sequential workflow that combined iterative story and storyboard development, still-image generation, image-to-video synthesis, and conventional post-production. ChatGPT supported iterative story, storyboard, and prompt development; GPT Image 2, Nano Banana Pro, and Nano Banana 2 were used to create still frames; and Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0 were used exclusively in image-to-video mode. Sprite and reference sheets anchored recurring character identities. Each shot passed through multiple generations, human selection, and retouching before motion synthesis. Adobe Premiere Pro and After Effects were used for editorial construction, stabilization, masking, compositing, tonal finishing, sound design, and mastering. The resulting workflow shows how generative systems can operate inside a conventional directorial process while narrative intention, continuity, performance, rhythm, and final assembly remain under human control.

items.title: A Reflection-Grounded Framework for AI Workflows and Assessment in Design Education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce polished personas, visual concepts, interface layouts, and design outputs, making final artefacts an increasingly unreliable indicator of students’ design understanding and contribution. This paper examines how assessment in design education can move beyond visual outcomes to evaluate the capabilities students exercise when working with generative AI. The study analyses 80 beginning-of-semester concept submissions and 79 end-of-semester reflections from an undergraduate design course, including 77 matched student pairs. Crucially, this setup allowed us to trace how workflows evolved as students transitioned from a mandated-AI conceptual phase to a free-choice prototyping phase. Through inductive coding and cross-stage qualitative comparison, findings show that students valued AI as a cognitive partner for early divergent exploration. However, many deliberately abandoned it during high-fidelity execution due to limited directability, generic outputs, cultural misrepresentation, and inefficiency. Based on these trajectories, we propose an assessment framework mapped to the Double Diamond design process. This framework derives seven assessable AI-era capabilities, enabling educators to evaluate design judgment, verification, and ethical responsibility rather than generated outputs alone.

items.title: A Review of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Implications for Employment and Economic Inequality
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming work environments through automated task execution, content generation, data analysis, and human–AI collaboration. This review examines its technological foundations, workplace adoption, implications for employment, and potential effects on economic inequality. It outlines major generative architectures, including generative adversarial networks, transformers, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, autoencoders, and autoregressive models, as well as applications in image, audio, video, and three-dimensional content generation. The review then considers how technological capabilities translate into employment outcomes through firm adoption, deployment depth, task reorganization, complementary investment, and labor reallocation. It also discusses the changing skills required in AI-enabled workplaces, emphasizing critical thinking, creativity, emotional intelligence, digital literacy, AI ethics, and human–machine collaboration. Furthermore, the paper explores how unequal access to AI technologies, occupational disruption, and concentrated economic benefits may widen disparities within and between countries. Ethical, security, bias, privacy, and interpretability challenges are also considered. Overall, the review highlights the need for workforce development, responsible AI governance, inclusive policies, and equitable access to ensure that GenAI supports productive, broadly shared socioeconomic progress across diverse sectors and communities amid changing economic conditions.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Systems Model of Remote Maritime Operations: Total Interpretive Structural Modelling of Human Capability, Situation Awareness and Navigation Safety
items.abstract: The shift to Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship (MASS) operations redistributes safety-critical functions among Remote Operation Centre (ROC) navigators, automation and digital systems. Yet, relationships among Operator Capability, cognition, work-system conditions and Navigation Safety remain insufficiently integrated. This study develops a literature-grounded socio-technical model using a 48-study systematic literature review, thematic synthesis, Total Interpretive Structural Modelling (TISM), MICMAC analysis, structural sensitivity analysis and preliminary expert review. Retrospective eligibility reassessment and author-confirmed source verification finalised the 48-study evidence base; historical screening and coding provenance was partially reconstructed. Eight elements were retained: Operator Capability, Situation Awareness (SA), Decision-Making Quality, Navigation Safety, Human–Machine Interface and Information/Data Conditions, Workload, Trust and Transparency, and Level of Automation. The six-level hierarchy places automation upstream of interface/information conditions; Operator Capability, workload and trust/transparency; SA; decision making; and Navigation Safety. SA is a cognitive state supporting decision making, with selected human and system conditions also modelled as direct influences. Downstream ordering persisted across contextual alternatives but changed when decision-making-to-SA feedback merged SA and decision making. The model represents structural reachability, not empirically established causality, mediation or predictive validity. Preliminary expert review informed refinement, not empirical validation. The model supports Goal-Directed Task Analysis, competency mapping and simulator-based ROC assessment.

items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
items.abstract: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: A Survey on Machine Learning Techniques for Building Advanced Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) represents an emerging paradigm in artificial intelligence that enables systems to operate autonomously, adapt to dynamic environments, and pursue complex goals with minimal human intervention. Unlike traditional AI systems that rely on predefined rules and supervised execution, Agentic AI integrates perception, reasoning, learning, and action to make intelligent decisions in real time. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Agentic AI systems, focusing on their architectural foundations, learning paradigms, and emerging application domains. The study examines key architectural frameworks, highlighting their capabilities and limitations. The paper also reviews recent advancements and applications of Agentic AI in manufacturing, cybersecurity, healthcare, enterprise automation, and distributed systems. A comparative analysis of existing literature identifies critical research gaps related to scalability, explainability, security, governance, and human–AI collaboration. This survey provides a structured overview of the current state of Agentic AI and serves as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand its architectures, capabilities, and application potential

items.title: Adaptability and Adaptivity in Manual Assembly Systems: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Abstract The expanding array of production variants and the shifting demographic and organizational landscapes demand flexible and adaptable assembly systems. In this context, adaptive systems that can dynamically adapt to changing requirements, user groups, and contextual conditions offer considerable potential. This study aims to analyze the current state of research on adaptive and adaptable manual assembly systems by conducting a systematic literature review (SLR). The objective of this analysis is twofold: first, to identify key influencing factors, and second, to determine existing research gaps. The findings of the present study indicate that previous research has predominantly centered on technological and ergonomic aspects, particularly cyber-physical systems, assistive technologies, and anthropometric workplace adaptation. Conversely, psychosocial influencing factors, such as individual stress, strain, and qualification diversity, have received minimal attention. The failure to consider these human-related variables represents a significant research gap, particularly with regard to the sustainable design of adaptive systems. A discrepancy emerges between the theoretical conceptualization of the concepts and their practical implementation. The study underscores the imperative for interdisciplinary research, integrating technical, psychological, and organizational perspectives, to achieve the full potential of adaptive systems. In summary, the text presents a series of specific recommendations for the advancement of adaptive manual assembly systems in both research and practice.
