items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students: a cross-sectional study across educational levels
items.abstract: Objective To examine educational-level differences in artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students, and the independent associations of AI anxiety with the two academic outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 1,168 music students from 14 Chinese universities across eight provinces and municipalities (824 undergraduates, 276 master’s students, and 68 doctoral students). Welch’s ANOVA, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), adjusted general linear models, and hierarchical multiple regression were used to examine group differences and associations. AI anxiety × educational-level interactions were also tested. Results Adjusted educational-level effects were small (partial η 2 = 0.017 for AI anxiety, 0.011 for academic engagement, and 0.012 for academic burnout; multivariate partial η 2 = 0.008 for engagement and burnout jointly). Adjusted comparisons showed differences among all three educational levels in AI anxiety. Undergraduates reported lower academic engagement than both postgraduate groups. For burnout, undergraduates scored higher than master’s students, while the undergraduate–doctoral difference was not significant. AI anxiety correlated negatively with academic engagement ( r = −0.166) and positively with academic burnout ( r = 0.361). After adjustment, AI anxiety remained negatively associated with engagement ( β = −0.141) and positively associated with burnout ( β = 0.332). Neither association varied significantly across educational levels. Conclusion Educational-level differences in AI anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout were small. AI anxiety was independently associated with both academic outcomes, with no significant moderation by educational level. These findings highlight the importance of considering students’ psychological experiences when integrating AI into higher music education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Renewable Energy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is recognized as a key enabler in handling the variability, intermittency, and nonlinear characteristics of renewable energy resources. This chapter presents a detailed review of AI-based approaches for the most prominent renewable energy systems, with a special focus on solar and wind energy systems. The chapter explores machine learning, deep learning, evolutionary algorithms, and hybrid intelligent models for the purposes of resource forecasting, system optimization, microgrid management, predictive maintenance, and smart grid integration. Furthermore, this chapter presents AI-based developments in photovoltaic systems, wind turbine control, virtual power plants, and energy storage management. However, issues associated with data quality, generalization, cybersecurity, and explainability still exist despite the significant progress achieved. In summary, the integration of AI with renewable energy systems represents a paradigm shift towards intelligent, autonomous, and resilient clean energy infrastructure, and it also reveals essential research directions to further accelerate sustainable energy transitions.

items.title: Artificial intelligence capability as a mediator between human resource management, logistics coordination, and flood response performance in Malaysia
items.abstract: Flood response requires coordinated organizational resources and appropriate technological capabilities. This study examined associations among human resource management (HRM), logistics coordination (LC), artificial intelligence capability (AIC), and flood response performance (FRP) among respondents involved in Malaysian flood-response activities. A cross-sectional survey conducted between September 2025 and February 2026 provided 593 responses. Questionnaire items were developed from a review of relevant literature. The revised analysis used observed mean composite scores, standardized ordinary least squares regression, and 3,000 bootstrap resamples to estimate direct and indirect associations. HRM and LC were positively associated with AIC, while AIC and LC were positively associated with FRP. Significant indirect associations through AIC were identified for HRM and LC. The direct HRM–FRP association was nonsignificant under bootstrap inference but significant under conventional regression inference, indicating sensitivity to the uncertainty estimation method. The findings provide preliminary evidence concerning organizational capabilities and perceived flood response performance. However, the cross-sectional design, purposive sampling, and absence of independent validation limit causal interpretation and generalizability.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Enabled Imaging Biomarkers for Distinguishing Pseudoprogression from True Progression after Cellular Immunotherapy in Glioblastoma
items.abstract: Abstract Pseudoprogression, transient radiographic worsening caused by treatment-related inflammation rather than tumor growth, is a well-recognized pitfall after chemoradiotherapy for glioblastoma and is becoming more relevant as checkpoint inhibitors and cellular immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells enter clinical testing. Conventional structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cannot reliably separate pseudoprogression from true progression, exposing patients to premature treatment discontinuation or unnecessary intensification. Quantitative, artificial-intelligence-based imaging analysis (radiomics, and its molecular extension radiogenomics) is an emerging candidate solution. In this narrative review we synthesize the evidence on radiomics and radiogenomics for differentiating pseudoprogression from true progression in glioblastoma, with emphasis on the immunotherapy and cellular-therapy context. We summarize the pathobiology and reported frequency of pseudoprogression after standard and immune-based therapies, outline the limitations of current response criteria (RANO, iRANO, RANO 2.0), and review representative studies of texture analysis, hand-crafted radiomics, deep-learning radiomics, and radiogenomics. Although several studies report promising discrimination (reported area-under-the-curve values of approximately 0.88-0.92 in different cohorts), the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, retrospective designs, inconsistent definitions and protocols, and infrequent external validation. Progress will require prospective multicenter cohorts with standardized acquisition and segmentation, adherence to TRIPOD and CLAIM reporting standards, transparent and interpretable models, and integration with clinical, molecular, and liquid-biopsy data. A dedicated evidence base specific to cellular immunotherapy is urgently needed.

items.abstract: In this era, the role of electric vehicles is increasing due to their advanced features. In the next transportation system, this emerging technique will play a vital role in every energy sector. The implementation of EVs is increasing due to their demand as the best infrastructure required for this field. An integration of EV with conventional and non- conventional energy sources provides the most sustainable and reliable EV module, which can enhance optimal production of electricity and smart mobility. Through the integration of AI with EVs provide them self-decision-making system. This is possible by providing insights into machine learning algorithms and real-time predictive modeling with proper battery management and a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) communication system. Further, an AI-driven EV module facilitates traffic management, autonomous driving, and predictive management, which turns into a smart mobility environment. After this, when such configurations integrate with the Internet of Things (IoT), it strengthens its mobility ecosystem. This makes an improvement in the charging infrastructure and the transportation planning system. So, in this chapter, we will describe current emerging trends in EVs with AI integration for energy management systems. Further, this chapter will focus on the performance of AI in handling mobility and transportation systems along with infrastructure.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Generating Drug-like Molecules: A Taxonomy of Methods and Evaluation Strategies
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in critical care: A narrative review on promise, progress, and challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.
